drill.title: Calibrate a thermometer in ice water
body: A thermometer is only useful if it tells the truth. Ice water is always 32°F, so it's the easiest way to check one. If yours reads a little off, you can fix it or remember how far off it is.
This week's drill has a second, short part: a quick review of knife safety, because this unit's recipes dice an onion or a pepper before the knife unit starts in week 9.
steps: Fill a tall glass to the top with ice. Add cold water until it's just below the ice, and stir. Wait 3 minutes so the water gets as cold as the ice.
Push the thermometer's stem into the middle of the glass, at least 2 inches deep. Don't let the tip touch the sides or the bottom.
Wait until the number stops changing, about 30 seconds for a digital one. It should read 32°F.

If it's off by more than 2°F, fix it: many digital thermometers have a reset or calibrate button (check its instructions), and a dial thermometer has a small nut under the dial that a grown-up can turn with pliers until the needle points to 32°F. If yours can't be fixed, write down how far off it is, and add or subtract that every time you use it.
Practice reading: check a glass of warm tap water and a glass of cold tap water. Write down all three numbers.
Wash the stem with hot, soapy water and dry it. Wash it after every use from now on, and before it goes into any food.

Knife safety review, 5 minutes. Set the cutting board on a damp paper towel so it can't slide. Hold the knife by its handle, never the blade. Hold the food with a claw: fingertips tucked under, knuckles in front.

Cut one onion in half through the root, lay each half flat side down, and chop it with the claw, sliding your hand back after each cut. Never wave a knife while you talk, and never try to catch a falling knife: step back and let it fall.
Use the onion this week, in shakshuka or another recipe.

quiz.q: What should a thermometer read in a glass of ice water?
quiz.explain: Water with ice in it stays at 32°F, the temperature where it freezes.

quiz.q: Where does the tip go when you check the ice water?
choices: In the middle of the glass, not touching the sides
Touching the bottom of the glass
Just under the top of the water
quiz.explain: The glass can be warmer than the water. The tip has to be in the water itself.

quiz.q: What do you do if a knife starts to fall?
choices: Step back and let it fall
Grab it as fast as you can
quiz.explain: A falling knife can cut you wherever you grab it. Let it land, then pick it up.

knowledge.title: Danger zone and how bacteria grow
body: Bacteria are tiny living things, far too small to see. Most are harmless, but some make people sick, and they can be on raw meat, eggs, and even vegetables. You can't see them, smell them, or taste them.

Bacteria grow fastest between 40°F and 140°F. That range is called the danger zone. In the middle of it, near body temperature, their numbers can double in as little as 20 minutes. At that rate, one becomes over a million in about 7 hours.

Cold slows them down: a fridge at 40°F or below keeps food safe for a few days, and a freezer at 0°F stops them growing at all (it doesn't kill them). Heat kills them: that's what the thermometer checks. Food kept hot stays safe at 140°F or above.

Some bacteria leave behind toxins that cooking doesn't destroy. So food that sat in the danger zone too long isn't made safe by heating it again. The rule: cooked food goes in the fridge within 2 hours, or within 1 hour on a hot day above 90°F.
steps: Put your thermometer in a glass of water and leave it on the middle shelf of your fridge for an hour. Write down what it reads. Is your fridge 40°F or below?
If you can, do the same in the freezer with the thermometer laid on a shelf. Is it 0°F or below?
Tell a grown-up if either one is too warm. Turning the dial a little colder usually fixes it.

quiz.q: What is the danger zone?
quiz.explain: Bacteria grow fastest between 40°F and 140°F.

quiz.q: How long can cooked food sit out on the counter?
choices: Up to 2 hours, or 1 hour on a hot day
quiz.explain: After that, bacteria may have grown enough to make someone sick, even if it's reheated.

quiz.q: What does the freezer do to bacteria?
choices: Stops them growing, but doesn't kill them
quiz.explain: Frozen food is safe while frozen. Once it thaws, the bacteria start growing again.

sabbath.title: Label and date containers
body: Getting ready for the Sabbath means food made ahead and kept in the fridge. A fridge full of unlabeled containers is a guessing game: what is it, and when was it made? A label answers both.
Most cooked food keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge. In the freezer it stays safe much longer, and tastes best within 2 to 3 months.
steps: Make a labeling kit: a roll of masking tape and a marker that won't smear. Keep them in a drawer near the fridge.
Label every container of leftovers from this week's cooking with what it is and the day it was cooked, like "Shakshuka, Sun 10/4".
Look through the fridge with a grown-up. Anything cooked more than 4 days ago gets thrown out.
Move the oldest food to the front so it gets eaten first.
Before the Sabbath, check that everything made for it is labeled.

quiz.q: How long do most cooked leftovers keep in the fridge?
quiz.explain: After about 4 days, throw it out, even if it looks and smells fine.

quiz.q: What goes on a label?
choices: What the food is and the day it was cooked
Only the name of the dish
quiz.explain: The date tells you how long it has left.

weeks.note: To 160°F

drill.title: Temp-check thick vs. thin patties
body: A thin patty and a thick one take very different times to cook through. This drill shows you how different, by cooking one of each side by side and checking both with the thermometer.
Buy an extra ½ pound of ground beef for it, or use two of this week's burger patties.
steps: Divide ½ pound of ground beef in half. Shape one half into a thin patty, about ¼ inch thick. Shape the other into a thick patty, about ¾ inch thick.
Wash your hands with soap, and wipe anything the raw beef touched.
Heat a skillet over medium-high heat with 1 teaspoon of oil until it shimmers. Lay both patties in with tongs. Wash the tongs and your hands.
Cook both until the bottoms are browned, then flip them. Start a timer.
After the flip, check each patty from the side every minute. Write down the time and temperature each time.
Take each patty off the heat as soon as it reads 160°F. Write down how many minutes each one took.
Turn off the stove. Compare: how much longer did the thick patty need? Did it look done before the thermometer said so?

quiz.q: Which patty needs longer to reach 160°F?
quiz.explain: Heat has farther to travel to reach the middle of a thick patty.

quiz.q: A burger is brown all the way through. Is it safe?
choices: Yes, if the juices are clear
quiz.explain: Ground beef can turn brown before it's hot enough to be safe. Only the thermometer can tell you.

knowledge.title: Safe internal temperatures chart
body: Each kind of food has a safe minimum temperature: the temperature that kills the harmful bacteria in it. The number goes in the thickest part, and the food has to reach it or go higher.

Poultry, any kind and any cut, ground or whole: 165°F. Ground beef and ground lamb: 160°F. Egg dishes: 160°F. Whole cuts of beef and lamb, like steaks and roasts: 145°F, then a 3-minute rest. Fish: 145°F. Leftovers and anything reheated: 165°F.

Why is ground beef hotter than steak? Bacteria live on the outside of meat. On a steak, the outside gets very hot, and the inside was never touched. Grinding mixes the outside all the way through, so the middle has to get hot too.
Taking the temperature: put the tip in the thickest part, away from bone and away from the pan. For a thin piece, go in from the side. Check more than one piece.
steps: Make a temperature card from memory, then check it against the list above: poultry 165°F, ground beef and lamb 160°F, eggs 160°F, whole cuts 145°F, fish 145°F, reheating 165°F.
Tape the card inside a cupboard door near the stove, where you'll see it when you cook.

quiz.q: What temperature is ground turkey safe at?
quiz.explain: Turkey is poultry, and all poultry is 165°F, even ground.

quiz.q: Why does ground beef need a higher temperature than a steak?
choices: Grinding mixes the bacteria from the outside all through it
quiz.explain: On a steak the bacteria stay on the outside, which gets hottest. Ground beef carries them into the middle.

quiz.q: What temperature do leftovers need when reheated?
quiz.explain: Reheated food goes all the way to 165°F.

sabbath.title: Cool a cooked dish in an ice bath
body: A big pot of hot food cools slowly. The middle can stay in the danger zone for hours, even in the fridge, and a hot pot warms everything around it. The safe way is to cool food fast: from 140°F down to 70°F within 2 hours, then down to 40°F within 4 more.
An ice bath does it quickly. So does dividing food into shallow containers, no more than 2 inches deep.
steps: Cook something to cool: a pot of soup, rice, or this week's leftovers warmed up, or cool a dish you're making ahead for the Sabbath.
Fill the sink or a large bowl partway with ice and cold water.
Move the hot food into a metal bowl or pot and set it in the ice water. The water should come up the sides but not spill in.
Stir every few minutes. Check the temperature in the middle every 10 minutes and write it down.
Once it reads 70°F or below, spoon it into shallow containers, cover them, label them, and put them in the fridge.
How long did it take to get from 140°F to 70°F?

quiz.q: How fast should hot food cool from 140°F to 70°F?
quiz.explain: Then it has 4 more hours to get to 40°F.

quiz.q: Why does a big pot of food cool slowly in the fridge?
choices: The middle holds its heat a long time
Fridges don't work on hot food
quiz.explain: Heat escapes from the outside. Shallow containers and ice baths give the middle less far to go.

weeks.note: From the rice cooked and cooled in the drill

drill.title: Safe cooling of a batch of rice, saved for the fried rice
body: Cooked rice is one of the riskiest leftovers. Raw rice can carry a germ that survives cooking, and if the cooked rice sits warm, it makes a toxin that reheating doesn't destroy. Rice that's cooled fast and kept cold is safe.
Do this drill the day before you cook this week's fried rice, and save the rice for it: fried rice needs cold, day-old rice.
steps: Cook 2 cups of white rice with 3 cups of water, the way you learned: rinse it, bring it to a boil, then cover it on low until the water is gone.
Spread the hot rice in a thin layer on a sheet pan with a spoon.
Leave it to cool, uncovered, until it stops steaming, about 20 minutes. Check the temperature in the middle of the layer.
Once it's below 70°F, or at most 1 hour after cooking, scoop it into a shallow container, cover it, and label it.
Put it in the fridge. Write down how long it took from the pot to the fridge.
Use it for the fried rice within a day or two.

quiz.q: Why is cooked rice spread out on a sheet pan?
choices: A thin layer cools much faster
quiz.explain: A thin layer loses heat quickly, so the rice spends very little time in the danger zone.

quiz.q: Rice sat out warm all afternoon. Will reheating make it safe?
choices: No, the toxin isn't destroyed by heat
quiz.explain: Throw it out. Some germs leave toxins that heat can't undo.

knowledge.title: Cross-contamination and board colors
body: Cross-contamination is when germs move from one food to another: from raw chicken to the salad, by way of a knife, a cutting board, or a hand. Cooking kills germs in the chicken, but the salad never gets cooked.

Many kitchens use cutting boards by color: red for raw meat, yellow for raw poultry, blue for raw fish, green for fruits and vegetables. At home, two boards is enough: one only for raw meat, poultry, and fish, and one for everything that won't be cooked.
With one board, cut in order: vegetables and anything eaten raw first, raw meat last. Then wash the board, the knife, and your hands with hot, soapy water.

Never rinse raw chicken in the sink: it splashes germs all over. Never put cooked food back on the plate that held it raw. Wash your hands after touching raw meat, eggs, or their packages, every time.
steps: Look at the cutting boards in your kitchen. With a grown-up, choose one for raw meat, poultry, and fish only. Mark it with a strip of tape or a sticker.
Walk through this week's recipe and find every step that touches raw chicken or raw egg. What touches it, and where is it washed?

quiz.q: You have one cutting board. What do you cut first?
choices: The vegetables, then the raw chicken
The raw chicken, then the vegetables
quiz.explain: Raw meat goes last, so its germs never touch food that won't be cooked.

quiz.q: Should you rinse raw chicken before cooking it?
choices: No, it splashes germs around the sink
quiz.explain: Rinsing doesn't make chicken safer. Cooking to 165°F does.

quiz.q: Grilled chicken is done. Where does it go?
choices: Back on the plate it came on raw
The cutting board you used for it raw
quiz.explain: The raw plate still has germs on it.

sabbath.title: Store a dish safely for the Sabbath
body: Food for the Sabbath is cooked before it begins. Some families serve it cold, and some keep dishes hot from before the Sabbath starts. Either way, the safety rules are the same: cold food stays at 40°F or below, and hot food stays at 140°F or above.
Dishes like chicken adobo get better after a day in the fridge, because the flavors soak in. They're good choices to make ahead.
steps: Choose a dish from this week to make ahead: the fried rice, chicken adobo, or another one your family will eat for the Sabbath.
Cook it Thursday or Friday. Cool it fast (week 2) in shallow containers.
Cover it, label it with the name and the day (week 1), and put it on a fridge shelf, not in the door, where it's warmer.
Check the fridge is at 40°F or below (week 1).
If your family keeps food hot for the Sabbath meal, check it with the thermometer before serving: 140°F or above.

quiz.q: Where in the fridge should make-ahead food go?
choices: On a shelf, not in the door
In the door, where it's easy to reach
quiz.explain: The door warms up every time it's opened.

quiz.q: Food kept hot for a meal needs to stay at what temperature?
quiz.explain: Below 140°F it's back in the danger zone.

weeks.note: Or beef kofta to 160°F, or turkey meatloaf to 165°F

drill.title: Set up a clean station unaided
body: A clean station is how every safe cook starts. This week you set one up on your own, the way you've practised. A grown-up watches and checks, but doesn't help.
steps: Clear the counter of everything you won't use. Wash it with hot, soapy water and dry it with a clean towel or paper towels.
Wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds, the time it takes to sing "Happy Birthday" twice.
Set out two cutting boards: the raw-meat board and the other one. Put a damp paper towel under each so it can't slide.
Set out a plate for raw meat, a separate clean plate for cooked food, and a bowl for scraps.
Put the thermometer where you can reach it, and check it in ice water (week 1).
Fill one side of the sink, or a dishpan, with hot, soapy water for washing as you go.
Have the grown-up check your station against this list. Then cook this week's recipe from it.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands?
quiz.explain: About as long as singing "Happy Birthday" twice.

quiz.q: Why are there two plates on the station?
choices: One for raw meat, one for cooked food
quiz.explain: Cooked food never goes back on the plate that held it raw.

knowledge.title: Food safety quiz
body: This quiz covers the whole unit: the danger zone, safe temperatures, cooling and storing, cross-contamination, and reheating. Try it without looking back. Then check any you missed in weeks 1 to 3.

quiz.q: What is the danger zone?
quiz.explain: Bacteria grow fastest between 40°F and 140°F.

quiz.q: What temperature is chicken safe at?
quiz.explain: All poultry, ground or whole, is 165°F.

quiz.q: What temperature is ground beef safe at?
quiz.explain: Ground beef and ground lamb are 160°F.

quiz.q: What does ice water read on a correct thermometer?
quiz.explain: Ice water is always 32°F, so it's how you check a thermometer.

quiz.q: How long can cooked food sit out before it goes in the fridge?
quiz.explain: After that, throw it out.

quiz.q: What's the fastest way to cool a pot of soup?
choices: Set it in an ice bath and stir, then use shallow containers
Put the whole pot in the fridge
Leave it on the stove overnight
quiz.explain: Food should drop from 140°F to 70°F within 2 hours.

quiz.q: You have one cutting board. In what order do you cut?
quiz.explain: Raw meat goes last, then the board is washed.

quiz.q: How hot should leftovers get when reheated?
quiz.explain: Reheated food goes all the way to 165°F.

quiz.q: How long do most cooked leftovers keep in the fridge?
quiz.explain: After about 4 days, throw them out.

quiz.q: Rice was left out warm all afternoon. What do you do?
quiz.explain: Some germs in rice leave toxins that reheating can't destroy.

sabbath.title: Reheat a stored dish to 165°F
body: Reheating stored food safely is the last skill of the unit. Leftovers go all the way to 165°F, checked in the middle of the thickest part. Warm isn't the same as hot enough.
Reheat only what you'll eat, and only once. Food reheated and cooled again loses quality and spends more time in the danger zone.
steps: Choose a stored dish: this week's meatloaf, or something you made ahead for the Sabbath.

Oven: put slices or portions in a baking dish with a splash of water or broth, cover with foil, and heat at 350°F. Microwave: cover the dish loosely and stop to stir or turn the food every minute or two.
Check the temperature in the middle of the thickest piece. It needs to read 165°F. If it doesn't, keep heating and check again.
Write down how long it took and how you heated it.
Do this before the Sabbath begins, for food your family will keep hot or serve.

quiz.q: How hot do reheated leftovers need to get?
quiz.explain: The middle heats last, so that's where the thermometer goes.

quiz.q: Why stir or turn food while it's in the microwave?
choices: Microwaves heat unevenly, leaving cold spots
To keep it from drying out
quiz.explain: Cold spots can stay in the danger zone even when other parts are hot.

recipes.title: Thick beef burgers
recipes.about: Thick, juicy beef burgers seared in a skillet and checked with a thermometer until they reach 160°F in the middle, on toasted buns.

recipes.title: Sandwich loaf
recipes.skill: Kneading to a windowpane, baking a loaf
recipes.about: A soft white sandwich loaf, kneaded until the dough stretches thin, proofed in a loaf pan, and baked to 190°F inside.

recipes.title: Dinner rolls
recipes.about: Soft, buttery pull-apart rolls, each weighed so they bake evenly, with a cold overnight proof so they're ready to bake.

recipes.title: Tabbouleh
recipes.about: A bright parsley salad with mint, tomato, and a little bulgur, dressed with lemon and olive oil. The knife work is the dish.

recipes.title: Israeli salad
recipes.about: Cucumber, tomato, and pepper diced small and even, with parsley, lemon, and olive oil.

recipes.title: Garlic green beans
recipes.about: Green beans blanched bright green, then sautéed in shimmering oil with garlic until just blistered.

recipes.title: Beef picadillo
recipes.about: Ground beef browned over a sofrito of onion, pepper, and garlic, simmered with tomato, raisins, and olives, over rice.

recipes.title: Cajun rice dressing with beef
recipes.about: Louisiana rice dressing: ground beef browned with onion, celery, and bell pepper, the pan deglazed, and cooked rice stirred through.

recipes.title: Rice pilaf
recipes.about: Long-grain rice toasted in butter with a few broken noodles, then simmered in broth until every grain is separate.

recipes.title: Roasted vegetables
recipes.skill: Even cuts that roast at the same rate
recipes.about: A sheet pan of carrots, potatoes, peppers, and onion, cut so they roast evenly and brown at the edges.

recipes.title: Roast chicken pieces
recipes.about: Bone-in chicken thighs and breasts roasted with herbs until crisp, each checked with a thermometer: 165°F.

recipes.title: Baked fish with lemon and herbs
recipes.skill: Baking fish gently, checking pin bones
recipes.about: Salmon, cod, or tilapia fillets baked with lemon, dill, and garlic until they flake and reach 145°F, with a side timed to finish at the same time.

recipes.title: Steamed fish with ginger and scallion
recipes.about: White fish fillets steamed on a plate in a covered pot, then topped with ginger, green onion, soy, and a little warm oil.

recipes.title: Cod poached in tomato sauce
recipes.about: Cod fillets poached gently in a garlicky tomato sauce with olives and capers until they flake.

recipes.title: Pan-seared trout
recipes.about: Trout fillets seared skin-side down until the skin is crisp, finished with butter and lemon.

recipes.title: Vegetable stock
recipes.about: A clear stock from onion, carrot, celery, and herbs, simmered gently, skimmed, and strained, for soups later.

recipes.title: Chicken stock
recipes.about: The carcass from week 28's roast chicken, or chicken wings or backs, simmered slowly with vegetables, strained, cooled fast, and the fat lifted off.

recipes.title: Beef tacos with pico de gallo
recipes.skill: An even dice for pico de gallo
recipes.about: Seasoned ground beef browned to 160°F in warm tortillas, topped with a fresh pico de gallo of diced tomato, onion, jalapeño, and cilantro.

recipes.title: Kuku sabzi
recipes.skill: A big pile of finely chopped herbs
recipes.about: A Persian herb frittata: parsley, cilantro, dill, and green onion chopped fine, bound with eggs, and baked until set at 160°F.

recipes.title: Cuban black beans and rice
recipes.skill: Soaking and simmering dried black beans
recipes.about: Dried black beans soaked, simmered until creamy, and finished with a sofrito of onion, pepper, and garlic, over rice.

recipes.title: Bulgur pilaf with chickpeas
recipes.skill: Toasting bulgur, then cooking it by absorption
recipes.about: Coarse bulgur toasted in olive oil with onion and tomato paste, then simmered in broth with chickpeas until the liquid is gone.
